title: iDRAC Login Failure
description: A single failed iDRAC login attempt (GUI, SSH, Redfish, or RACADM-over-network). The atomic building block for the brute-force/spray/successful-after-failures detections below. iDRAC is out-of-band management — it operates independently of the host OS's own power state, so authentication events here are visible even when the managed server itself is powered off.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Login attempt records with source, protocol, and outcome.

detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for authentication failure events across all access protocols.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Failed"
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, interface
tuning_guidance: Expect routine noise; use IDRAC-002/003 for volume-based detection.
investigation_steps: Confirm src_ip is a known out-of-band management source.
response_guidance: No action for an isolated failure.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated iDRAC Login Failures / Brute Force
description: Five or more failed iDRAC login attempts within 10 minutes. Because iDRAC is Tier-0/Tier-1 out-of-band infrastructure that can bypass the operating system entirely (power, console, firmware, boot control), this deserves the same low alert threshold as a domain controller or a hypervisor management interface.
detection_logic: Counts failed iDRAC logins per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count, dc(user) as distinct_users, values(src_ip) as source_ips by host, _time
| where count>=5
tuning_guidance: Minimal legitimate tuning expected; out-of-band management interfaces should see a small, predictable volume of authentication traffic.
investigation_steps: Validate targeted usernames.
Check for a subsequent success (IDRAC-004).
response_guidance: Block the source at the OOB network layer; this interface should never be reachable from a general-purpose network segment in the first place.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Password Spraying Across Fleet
description: A single source IP attempts authentication against many distinct iDRAC devices or usernames in a short window — consistent with an attacker who has obtained a candidate password (default credential lists, breach data) and is sweeping the out-of-band management network for any device it works on.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: LC log, category=Audit, aggregated across devices
data_sources.description: Authentication failures across the managed fleet.

detection_logic: Counts distinct target devices/usernames attempted per source IP across the fleet in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(host) as distinct_devices, dc(user) as distinct_users by src_ip, _time
| where distinct_devices>=5 OR distinct_users>=6
tuning_guidance: Exclude known vulnerability-scanning/asset-discovery source IPs operating on the OOB network under an approved schedule.
investigation_steps: Identify every targeted device.
Check for any success from the source (IDRAC-004).
response_guidance: Block the source at the OOB network layer immediately; treat as a fleet-wide credential-guessing campaign.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful iDRAC Login Following Repeated Failures
description: A successful iDRAC login for a user/device pair that had five or more failures in the preceding 30 minutes. Given that iDRAC compromise grants power, console, firmware, and boot-level control that bypasses the operating system entirely, this ranks among the single highest-priority detections in the entire catalogue.
detection_logic: Joins a failed-login threshold search with a subsequent success for the same user/device within 30 minutes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login"
| eval outcome=if(result="Failed","fail","success")
| transaction user, host maxspan=30m startswith=eval(outcome="fail") endswith=eval(outcome="success")
| where eventcount>=6
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate given how tightly OOB management access should normally be scoped.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Immediately check for virtual media mounts, boot overrides, firmware changes, and new user creation in the same session (IDRAC-020, IDRAC-030, IDRAC-050, IDRAC-010).
response_guidance: Disable the account, disconnect any active session (console/virtual media), and audit every action taken during the session before doing anything else — this session may have already achieved boot-level persistence.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Login From First-Seen Source IP
description: A successful iDRAC login from a source IP never seen for that device in the prior 30 days. OOB management networks typically have a small, static set of legitimate administrative sources (jump hosts, a dedicated management VLAN), making first-seen events unusually high-signal compared to general IT infrastructure.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Login success events with source IP.

detection_logic: Builds a 30-day baseline of source IPs per device and flags first-seen values.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Success"
| lookup idrac_source_baseline.csv host src_ip OUTPUT is_known
| where isnull(is_known)
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Maintain idrac_source_baseline.csv via a nightly scheduled search rather than an inline subsearch, given the value of this signal on Tier-0 infrastructure.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the administrator directly.
Verify the source is on the designated OOB management network at all.
response_guidance: Suspend the session pending confirmation if unexpected; any source outside the OOB management network warrants immediate escalation regardless of credential validity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Login Outside the Out-of-Band Management Network
description: A successful iDRAC login whose source IP falls outside the CIDR range(s) of the designated out-of-band management network. iDRAC (like the shared-LOM configuration it can be set to) should in a properly-segmented environment never be reachable from general-purpose production/user networks — a login from outside the OOB range is a strong signal that segmentation has failed or was never correctly implemented.
detection_logic: Compares login source IP against a maintained lookup of approved OOB management CIDR ranges.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Success"
| lookup idrac_oob_cidrs.csv src_ip OUTPUT is_oob_range
| where isnull(is_oob_range)
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Maintain the OOB CIDR allowlist; review whenever new management jump hosts or VPN pools are added.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the iDRAC's NIC is in dedicated or shared-LOM mode (IDRAC-041) — shared mode is far more likely to expose it to a general network.
response_guidance: Treat as Critical: this indicates either a network segmentation failure or unauthorized access, and both require immediate remediation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Default Credential Login Attempt
description: A login attempt (successful or failed) using iDRAC's well-known factory-default account (historically `root`/`calvin` on older iDRAC generations). Default-credential sweeps against exposed iDRACs are one of the most consistently observed opportunistic attack patterns against Dell server fleets in the wild, and a successful login here means the device was never hardened after deployment.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Login attempts using known default account names.

detection_logic: Filters login events for the well-known default username(s), regardless of outcome.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" user="root"
| lookup idrac_default_creds_flag.csv host OUTPUT still_default
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, result, still_default
tuning_guidance: If `still_default` is unknown, treat every successful login on this account as an emergency until you have positively confirmed the default password was rotated during provisioning.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the default password was actually changed for this device.
If the login succeeded and the password was still default, treat as a confirmed exposure.
response_guidance: Rotate the credential immediately regardless of outcome and audit the device for any changes made during a successful session.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC SSH or RACADM Remote Authentication
description: An administrative session is authenticated via SSH or remote RACADM rather than the HTTPS GUI or Redfish API. Tracked separately since CLI/RACADM sessions run raw commands that are individually less visible than GUI-driven actions in structured logs.
detection_logic: Filters login events for the SSH/RACADM interface.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Success" interface IN ("SSH","RACADM")
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, interface
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected automation source IPs (deployment tooling, OpenManage Enterprise) separately from interactive administrators.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference src_ip against the automation/jump-host allowlist.
response_guidance: No automatic action for expected sources; investigate per IDRAC-006 if outside the OOB network.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Session From Dormant or Service Account
description: A successful iDRAC login using an account that has not authenticated in 90+ days, or a service/automation account (normally used only for API-driven, non-interactive access) authenticating interactively via the GUI or console.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Login events cross-referenced against last-seen and account-type lookups.

detection_logic: Joins login success against a last-authenticated-date lookup and an account-type (interactive vs. service) lookup.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="Login" result="Success"
| lookup idrac_last_seen.csv host user OUTPUT last_seen
| lookup idrac_account_type.csv user OUTPUT account_type
| eval days_dormant=round((now()-strptime(last_seen,"%Y-%m-%d"))/86400,0)
| where days_dormant>=90 OR (account_type="service" AND interface="GUI")
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, days_dormant, account_type
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained last-seen lookup, ideally refreshed nightly.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account owner initiated this session.
For a service account used interactively, verify whether its credential may have been extracted and reused by a human operator.
response_guidance: Disable dormant accounts that should have been offboarded; investigate service-account interactive use as a likely credential-theft indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New iDRAC User Created
description: A new local iDRAC user account is created. Legitimate during provisioning, but also the most direct persistence mechanism available to an attacker who has gained administrative access to out-of-band management infrastructure.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for user-creation events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="UserCreated"
| table _time, host, user, acting_user
tuning_guidance: Correlate with change-management tickets or OpenManage Enterprise-driven provisioning workflows.
investigation_steps: Verify against an approved-accounts list.
Check the privilege level assigned (IDRAC-011).
response_guidance: Disable/delete immediately if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC User Granted Administrator Privilege
description: A user account (new or existing) is granted the Administrator privilege level, iDRAC's highest role, capable of every action this catalogue covers — power control, virtual media, firmware, boot configuration, and further account management.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for privilege-level changes to Administrator.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="UserPrivilegeChanged" privilege="Administrator"
| table _time, host, user, acting_user
tuning_guidance: No routine tuning — every occurrence should map to a change record.
investigation_steps: Verify against change management.
Review what the account does immediately afterward.
response_guidance: Downgrade immediately if unauthorized; treat as a Critical management-plane-compromise indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC User Deleted or Disabled
description: An account is deleted or disabled. Can be routine offboarding, or an attacker removing legitimate administrators' access to hinder incident response after establishing their own persistence account.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for user deletion/disable events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit (event="UserDeleted" OR event="UserDisabled")
| table _time, host, user, acting_user
tuning_guidance: Correlate with offboarding workflows for routine cases.
investigation_steps: Confirm against offboarding records.
Check for a corresponding new-account-creation event around the same time (account swap pattern).
response_guidance: Investigate if unaccounted for, particularly if it removes a legitimate security-team account.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Password Policy or Account Lockout Threshold Weakened
description: The account lockout threshold, minimum password complexity, or session-idle timeout policy is weakened. Directly enables the brute-force/spray scenarios detected elsewhere in this catalogue (IDRAC-002/003) to succeed with less resistance.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for authentication-policy configuration changes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("LockoutThreshold","PasswordComplexity","SessionTimeout")
| table _time, host, acting_user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for a documented troubleshooting scenario — require a change ticket and time-box any weakening.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Check for a subsequent brute-force/spray attempt (IDRAC-002/003).
response_guidance: Revert to organizational standard immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556.004: Network Device Authentication

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Directory Service (AD/LDAP) Authentication Changed
description: The Active Directory/LDAP configuration used for centralized iDRAC authentication is modified — server address, bind credentials, or role-group mapping. An attacker who controls this configuration can point authentication at a rogue directory server, or broaden a role-group mapping to grant iDRAC Administrator privilege to a directory group they already control.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for AD/LDAP configuration changes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("ADServerAddress","LDAPServerAddress","ADRoleGroup","LDAPBindDN")
| table _time, host, acting_user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during planned identity-infrastructure migrations; require a change ticket, especially for role-group mapping changes.
investigation_steps: Verify the new server/group against known-good directory infrastructure.
Audit all logins relying on this trust since the change.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized changes immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556.004: Network Device Authentication

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Local Authentication Fallback Enabled Over Directory
description: Local-account fallback authentication is enabled on a device where centralized AD/LDAP authentication is the expected mechanism, or the fallback broadens beyond a declared break-glass account. Bypasses centralized MFA and identity-governance controls in favor of locally-managed, often weaker-governed credentials.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for local-authentication-fallback enablement.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="LocalAuthFallback" cfgattr_value="Enabled"
| table _time, host, acting_user
tuning_guidance: A single declared break-glass account with local fallback is normal; broadening beyond that is not.
investigation_steps: Confirm this matches the declared break-glass procedure.
response_guidance: Restrict fallback to the single documented break-glass account if broadened.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Console Session Started
description: A Virtual Console (KVM-over-IP) session is started, giving the operator interactive keyboard/video/mouse access to the managed server as if physically present at the console — including access to BIOS setup, boot menus, and any unlocked OS session, entirely bypassing normal network-based access controls on the host. This is one of the highest-value capabilities iDRAC exposes and the baseline detection for the higher-priority console detections below.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for Virtual Console session-start events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart"
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected administrator source IPs and typical session frequency per device; console access should be infrequent on most production servers outside maintenance windows.
investigation_steps: Confirm the session against a change ticket or known maintenance activity.
Check session duration and any subsequent BIOS/boot/media changes (IDRAC-021 through IDRAC-024).
response_guidance: No automatic action for expected sessions; escalate per the more specific console detections below for anomalous ones.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Console Session From Unusual Source or Outside Maintenance Window
description: A Virtual Console session originates from a source IP not on the known-administrator baseline, or starts outside a declared maintenance window. Given the console's ability to bypass every OS-level control, an unexplained session here deserves elevated scrutiny even without any further suspicious activity.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Console session events cross-referenced against a source baseline and maintenance-window lookup.

detection_logic: Joins console session-start events against a source-IP baseline and a maintenance-window lookup.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart"
| lookup idrac_source_baseline.csv host src_ip OUTPUT is_known
| lookup idrac_maintenance_windows.csv host _time OUTPUT in_window
| where isnull(is_known) OR isnull(in_window)
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Maintain both lookups; without them this degrades to a high-volume, low-precision alert.
investigation_steps: Confirm against change management.
Review the full session for BIOS/boot/media changes.
response_guidance: Terminate the session and investigate if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multiple Concurrent iDRAC Virtual Console Sessions
description: More than one Virtual Console session is active on the same device simultaneously — unusual for routine single-operator maintenance and potentially indicating either a shared/compromised credential being used by two parties at once, or an attacker's session running alongside a legitimate administrator's.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Overlapping console session start/end events per device.

detection_logic: Identifies overlapping session-start/end intervals for the same device.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit (event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart" OR event="VirtualConsoleSessionEnd")
| transaction host maxevents=2 startswith=eval(event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart")
| where mvcount(user)>1
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Some organizations legitimately allow shared/collaborative console sessions for training or paired troubleshooting — exclude those known scenarios.
investigation_steps: Identify both sessions' source IPs and users.
Confirm both are authorized.
response_guidance: Terminate any unconfirmed session immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Console Access Immediately Followed by Reboot
description: A Virtual Console session is followed within minutes by a power-cycle/reset action on the same device — consistent with an operator making a BIOS/boot change interactively via console and then rebooting to apply it, which is exactly the workflow an attacker would use to weaken boot security and then reboot into the modified state.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Console session events correlated with subsequent power-action events.

detection_logic: Correlates a console session-start event with a subsequent power-cycle/reset event on the same device within 15 minutes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit
| eval stage=case(event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart","1_console_access", event="PowerControl" AND (action="Reset" OR action="PowerCycle"),"2_reboot", 1==1, null())
| where isnotnull(stage)
| transaction host maxspan=15m startswith=eval(stage="1_console_access")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=2
| table _time, host, user, stage
tuning_guidance: Common, benign pattern during routine maintenance (applying an update, changing a setting) — pair with IDRAC-024 (boot config change) to raise confidence this was a security-relevant change rather than routine work.
investigation_steps: Check whether a boot configuration or BIOS change occurred during the console session (IDRAC-024/IDRAC-032).
response_guidance: Investigate further if combined with an unconfirmed console session or a boot/BIOS change; otherwise treat as routine.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Console Access Followed by BIOS Setting or Virtual Media Change
description: A Virtual Console session is followed by a BIOS configuration change or virtual media mount during the same session. This is the core high-priority console attack pattern this catalogue is built to catch: console access alone is a capability, but console access immediately preceding a security-relevant configuration change is a strong signal of active, hands-on-keyboard tampering.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Console session correlated with subsequent BIOS/virtual-media configuration events.

detection_logic: Correlates a console session-start event with a subsequent BIOS setting change or virtual media attach event on the same device within the session window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit
| eval stage=case(event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart","1_console_access", event="BIOSConfigChange" OR event="VirtualMediaAttached","2_config_change", 1==1, null())
| where isnotnull(stage)
| transaction host maxspan=30m startswith=eval(stage="1_console_access")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=2
| table _time, host, user, stage
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during planned BIOS updates or OS deployment via mounted media — cross-reference against a change ticket before escalating.
investigation_steps: Identify exactly what BIOS setting or media was changed.
Confirm against a change ticket.
response_guidance: If unconfirmed, treat as active tampering: isolate the device from remote management and investigate immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

threshold.baseline_condition: console session -> BIOS change or virtual media mount

title: Unusually Long iDRAC Virtual Console Session
description: A Virtual Console session remains open significantly longer than typical maintenance activity for the device — a soft signal that may indicate the console is being used for extended interactive access (e.g. active reconnaissance or staged multi-step tampering) rather than a discrete maintenance task.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Session start/end pairs with computed duration.

detection_logic: Computes session duration from paired start/end events and flags outliers against the device's own historical baseline.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit (event="VirtualConsoleSessionStart" OR event="VirtualConsoleSessionEnd")
| transaction host user maxevents=2
| eval duration_min=round(duration/60,1)
| where duration_min>=120
tuning_guidance: Some legitimate OS installation/deployment workflows via console genuinely take hours — exclude known deployment automation patterns.
investigation_steps: Review what activity occurred throughout the session if other detections fired during it.
response_guidance: Use as a contributing signal only; not independently actionable.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Media Attached
description: A virtual CD/DVD, USB image, or floppy is attached via iDRAC's Virtual Media capability, presenting it to the host operating system exactly as a physically-inserted device would. This is treated as a potential payload-delivery/OS-bypass mechanism throughout this catalogue: it lets an operator (or attacker) introduce arbitrary bootable or file-system content to the server without ever touching the datacenter floor.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Virtual media attach events with source URI/image.

detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for virtual media attach events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="VirtualMediaAttached"
| table _time, host, user, media_type, source_uri
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected deployment-automation source URIs (e.g. a known OS-deployment image repository) separately from ad hoc interactive mounts.
investigation_steps: Identify the source_uri — is it a known, trusted image repository?
Check whether a boot-order change and reboot followed (IDRAC-031/IDRAC-024).
response_guidance: If unconfirmed, treat as a potential payload-delivery attempt: detach the media and investigate the mounting session immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: ATT&CK has no dedicated technique for remotely-mounted virtual/emulated media specifically. T1200 (Hardware Additions) is the closest documented analogue — an iDRAC-mounted virtual CD/USB image is presented to the host exactly as a physically-inserted device would be, achieving the same effect (introducing attacker-controlled media the OS will recognize) without physical presence. Used here with this explicit caveat per specification quality-control rule #6.

title: iDRAC Virtual Media From Unusual or External URI
description: A virtual media attach event references a source URI outside the organization's known, approved image repositories — particularly one resolving to an external network. Since the mounted image is fetched by the iDRAC itself (often over HTTP/HTTPS/CIFS/NFS/SMB), an externally-hosted image is functionally equivalent to an attacker delivering a payload directly onto the server's virtual media bus.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Virtual media attach events with source URI, cross-referenced against an approved-repository allowlist.

detection_logic: Joins virtual media attach events against a maintained allowlist of approved image repository hostnames/CIDR ranges.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="VirtualMediaAttached"
| rex field=source_uri "://(?<uri_host>[^/]+)"
| lookup idrac_approved_media_sources.csv uri_host OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, host, user, source_uri, uri_host
tuning_guidance: Maintain the approved-repository allowlist tightly — this should be a small, well-known set of internal deployment servers.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident pending confirmation.
Identify the URI's ownership and reachability.
response_guidance: Detach the media immediately and isolate the device from remote management if the source is unconfirmed or external.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1105: Ingress Tool Transfer

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Virtual Media Mount Followed by One-Time Boot Override and Reboot
description: The flagship attack chain this catalogue is built around, named explicitly by the specification as the highest priority available: a virtual media mount, followed by a one-time boot-device override pointing at that media, followed by a reboot. This sequence lets an attacker boot the server directly into attacker-controlled media — bypassing the installed operating system, its authentication, its logging, and any endpoint protection running on it entirely.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Virtual media, boot-override, and power-action events for the same device within a short window.

detection_logic: Correlates a virtual media attach event with a subsequent one-time boot-override event targeting virtual media, followed by a power-cycle/reset, all on the same device within 20 minutes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit
| eval stage=case(event="VirtualMediaAttached","1_media_mounted", event="BootOverride" AND boot_device IN ("VCD-DVD","vFDD","Virtual Optical Drive"),"2_boot_override", event="PowerControl" AND (action="Reset" OR action="PowerCycle"),"3_reboot", 1==1, null())
| where isnotnull(stage)
| transaction host maxspan=20m startswith=eval(stage="1_media_mounted")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=3
| table _time, host, user, stage
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for planned OS installation/recovery workflows — require this exact sequence to correlate with a change ticket; treat any unticketed occurrence as an emergency regardless of time of day.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident: the server may currently be booted into attacker-controlled media.
Do not assume the installed OS is still trustworthy once this sequence completes unconfirmed.
response_guidance: Power off the device immediately if the sequence is unconfirmed, detach the media, and treat the host OS as compromised pending full forensic imaging — a full rebuild may be warranted depending on findings.
author: Threat Detection Library

threshold.baseline_condition: virtual media mount -> one-time boot override to media -> reboot

title: iDRAC Virtual Media Mounted by Unusual Administrator
description: A virtual media attach event is performed by an account not on the small, expected list of administrators who routinely handle OS deployment/recovery media mounts for this device.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Virtual media events cross-referenced against an expected-operator baseline.

detection_logic: Joins virtual media attach events against a lookup of accounts expected to perform media operations.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="VirtualMediaAttached"
| lookup idrac_media_operators.csv user OUTPUT is_expected_operator
| where isnull(is_expected_operator)
| table _time, host, user, source_uri
tuning_guidance: Maintain the expected-operator lookup; particularly valuable in larger environments where media operations are normally handled by a small deployment/imaging team.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification with the account owner.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed; treat consistently with IDRAC-031 if the account is also unfamiliar.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Power Action Outside Maintenance Window
description: A power off, power cycle, hard reset, or NMI action is issued via iDRAC outside a declared maintenance window. Since iDRAC power control operates independently of the OS (it can forcibly power off a host regardless of what's running), this is a direct denial-of-service/disruption capability that deserves scrutiny whenever it falls outside expected change activity.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Power control action events cross-referenced against a maintenance-window lookup.

detection_logic: Filters power-control events against a maintenance-window lookup.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="PowerControl"
| lookup idrac_maintenance_windows.csv host _time OUTPUT in_window
| where isnull(in_window)
| table _time, host, user, action
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained maintenance-window lookup; without it, expect noise from legitimate ad hoc operations support.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification with the acting administrator.
Check for a preceding console/media/BIOS change (IDRAC-023/024/032).
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed; escalate immediately if combined with any of the sequence detections above.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Multiple Power Cycles in Short Window
description: A device is power-cycled multiple times within a short window — consistent with either a hardware fault loop or an operator repeatedly testing a change (e.g. a boot configuration) via reboot, both of which warrant investigation for different reasons.
detection_logic: Counts power-cycle/reset events per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="PowerControl" action IN ("Reset","PowerCycle")
| bin _time span=30m
| stats count by host, _time
| where count>=3
tuning_guidance: Exclude devices under known active hardware troubleshooting.
investigation_steps: Check SEL for hardware fault indicators (IDRAC-070+) vs. a pattern of deliberate configuration testing.
response_guidance: Investigate as a hardware issue or, if paired with other console/boot detections, as active tampering.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Mass Power Action Across Multiple iDRAC-Managed Servers
description: The same administrator or source IP issues power-off/power-cycle actions against an unusually large number of distinct servers within a short window — a fleet-wide denial-of-service scenario and one of the clearest possible signals of iDRAC management-plane compromise being used for maximum-impact disruption (e.g. a ransomware-adjacent extortion tactic of powering off an entire datacenter row).

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: LC log, category=Audit, aggregated across devices
data_sources.description: Power control events across the managed fleet.

detection_logic: Counts distinct devices power-actioned per acting user/source in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="PowerControl" action IN ("PowerOff","Reset","PowerCycle")
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(host) as distinct_devices, values(host) as devices by user, src_ip, _time
| where distinct_devices>=5
tuning_guidance: Baseline your organization's normal fleet-power-action scope (some environments legitimately do rolling fleet reboots for patching) and tune the threshold accordingly.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live fleet-wide incident.
Identify every affected device and the acting identity's authorization scope.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, this is an active availability incident: suspend the acting account/source immediately and begin fleet-wide status verification.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC One-Time Boot Override to Network (PXE) Boot
description: A one-time boot override is set to PXE/network boot. Combined with control over the network segment the server will PXE-boot from (or a rogue DHCP/TFTP server), this can be used to boot the server into attacker-supplied OS/recovery media without ever touching virtual media at all.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for boot-override events targeting network/PXE boot.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="BootOverride" boot_device="NIC"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for automated OS deployment/imaging pipelines (PXE-based provisioning) — allowlist known deployment automation accounts.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Check whether the PXE/DHCP infrastructure the device will boot from is trusted.
response_guidance: Revert the override if unauthorized before the next reboot occurs.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: No dedicated ATT&CK technique exists for out-of-band boot-device override specifically; T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) is used as the closest-fit parent technique per the master specification's guidance to use the nearest valid technique with an explicit caveat where ATT&CK does not cleanly represent firmware/boot activity.

title: iDRAC Boot Order (BIOS Boot Sequence) Changed
description: The persistent (not one-time) BIOS boot device sequence is modified — a more durable version of the one-time override that will affect every subsequent boot until changed back, potentially establishing long-term boot-level persistence.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for persistent boot-sequence configuration changes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="BootSeq"
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during planned hardware/OS migrations; require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Verify the new boot order matches the intended configuration.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized changes.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-037.

title: iDRAC UEFI/Legacy Boot Mode Changed
description: The boot mode is switched between UEFI and legacy BIOS. Switching from UEFI to legacy can silently disable Secure Boot (which is UEFI-only) as a side effect, without Secure Boot's own setting necessarily appearing to change — a subtle way to weaken boot integrity protection.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for boot-mode configuration changes to Bios (legacy).
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="BootMode" cfgattr_value="Bios"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for compatibility with legacy OS/hardware requirements — require documented justification given the Secure Boot implication.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether Secure Boot was enabled prior to this change (IDRAC-040) and verify its status after.
response_guidance: Revert to UEFI mode and re-verify Secure Boot status unless explicitly justified.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-037.

title: iDRAC Secure Boot Disabled
description: UEFI Secure Boot is disabled. Secure Boot cryptographically verifies the bootloader and OS kernel before execution — disabling it removes the primary control preventing an unsigned/tampered bootloader (including one delivered via the virtual-media attack chain, IDRAC-032) from executing. One of the explicitly highest-priority detections named in the specification.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for Secure Boot configuration changes to Disabled.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="SecureBoot" cfgattr_value="Disabled"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: No routine legitimate case for disabling Secure Boot on a production server outside a documented, rare compatibility exception — treat every occurrence as requiring explicit justification.
investigation_steps: Identify who disabled it and cross-reference against a change ticket.
Check for a subsequent virtual media mount or boot override (IDRAC-030/037) — this combination is the direct enabler of an unsigned-bootloader attack.
response_guidance: Re-enable immediately unless explicitly authorized; treat as Critical if combined with any virtual-media or boot-override activity.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-037; Secure Boot exists specifically to prevent the Pre-OS Boot tampering this technique family describes.

title: iDRAC TPM Disabled or Cleared
description: The Trusted Platform Module is disabled, or its state is cleared (wiping stored keys/measurements). TPM clearing invalidates any disk-encryption keys sealed to it (e.g. BitLocker) and resets the hardware root of trust used for measured boot — an attacker who can clear the TPM can potentially force a re-provisioning flow or break the chain of trust the OS relies on to detect boot-time tampering.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for TPM disable or clear events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("TpmSecurity","TpmClear")
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: No routine legitimate case outside a documented hardware-replacement or re-provisioning procedure.
investigation_steps: Confirm against change management immediately.
If TPM was cleared, coordinate with the OS/disk-encryption team — data may become inaccessible without a recovery key.
response_guidance: Treat as Critical: this can be both a security-control-weakening action and a destructive one simultaneously.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: No dedicated ATT&CK technique exists for TPM state tampering specifically; T1495 (Firmware Corruption) is used as the closest-fit technique for hardware-root-of-trust impairment, per the specification's guidance to use the nearest valid technique with an explicit caveat.

title: iDRAC BIOS Setup Password Removed
description: The BIOS/UEFI setup password is removed, which (where configured) is a secondary control against unauthorized boot-configuration changes even for someone with iDRAC console access. Its removal widens who can subsequently change boot order, Secure Boot, or TPM settings via the console.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for BIOS setup password removal events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="SetupPassword" cfgattr_value=""
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during a documented password-reset procedure — require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Reinstate a new password promptly if this was a legitimate reset.
response_guidance: Reinstate the BIOS password if removal was unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-037.

title: iDRAC Virtualization or IOMMU Security Setting Weakened
description: CPU virtualization extensions (VT-x/AMD-V) or IOMMU (VT-d/AMD-Vi) settings are disabled. On a hypervisor host these underpin VM isolation and device-passthrough protection — weakening them can undermine the isolation guarantees between guest VMs or between a VM and the host.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for virtualization/IOMMU BIOS setting changes to Disabled.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("ProcVirtualization","IoatDma","SriovGlobalEnable") cfgattr_value="Disabled"
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for non-hypervisor bare-metal workloads that don't require virtualization extensions — verify the device's actual role before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether this host runs a hypervisor.
Check business justification for the change.
response_guidance: Re-enable if the host runs a hypervisor and the change was unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1611: Escape to Host

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Firmware Downgrade
description: iDRAC's own firmware is downgraded to an older version. Firmware downgrades can reintroduce previously-patched vulnerabilities, strip newer security-hardening defaults, and are a documented technique for re-exposing a known exploit path against out-of-band management controllers specifically — one of the highest-priority firmware detections named in the specification.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Firmware update events with old/new version and update source.

detection_logic: Filters firmware update events and flags version-downgrade cases via semantic version comparison.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="FirmwareUpdate" component="iDRAC"
| eval is_downgrade=if(cmp_version(old_version,new_version)>0,1,0)
| where is_downgrade=1
| table _time, host, user, old_version, new_version, update_source
tuning_guidance: Use a proper semantic-version comparison function (illustrated here as `cmp_version`, implement via a lookup table or custom command) — naive string comparison will misorder versions like 6.10 vs 6.9.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a change ticket for planned downgrades (e.g. rolling back a known-bad update).
Verify the source of the firmware image and whether Dell's digital signature validation passed.
response_guidance: Treat unauthorized downgrades as Critical defense evasion; re-upgrade and audit configuration/accounts for tampering introduced during the downgraded window.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601.002: Downgrade System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Unsigned or Firmware Validation Failure
description: A firmware update package fails Dell's digital signature/validation check. A rejected update is the expected, working-as-intended outcome, but repeated failures — or, worse, any evidence the validation step itself was bypassed — deserve investigation into where the untrusted firmware image originated.
detection_logic: Filters firmware update events for validation-failure outcomes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="FirmwareUpdate" result="ValidationFailed"
| table _time, host, user, component, update_source
tuning_guidance: Low false-positive rate; investigate every occurrence.
investigation_steps: Identify the update_source and who initiated the update.
Confirm no bypass of validation occurred despite the failure being logged.
response_guidance: Investigate the source of the rejected firmware image; treat as a potential supply-chain or tampering attempt.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Firmware Update From Unexpected Source
description: A firmware update is applied from a source URI/location outside the organization's approved update repositories (e.g. Dell's own update service, an internal OpenManage Enterprise-managed catalog, or a designated internal repository).
detection_logic: Joins firmware update events against an approved-source allowlist.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="FirmwareUpdate"
| lookup idrac_approved_fw_sources.csv update_source OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, host, user, update_source, component
tuning_guidance: Maintain the approved-source allowlist tightly.
investigation_steps: Verify the source's legitimacy before the update completes if caught in progress.
response_guidance: Halt/reject the update if the source is unconfirmed; audit the device afterward if it already completed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Firmware Update Outside Maintenance Window
description: A firmware update (of iDRAC itself, BIOS, NIC, RAID/PERC controller, or PSU) occurs outside a declared maintenance window.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Firmware update events cross-referenced against a maintenance-window lookup.

detection_logic: Joins firmware update events against a maintenance-window lookup.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="FirmwareUpdate"
| lookup idrac_maintenance_windows.csv host _time OUTPUT in_window
| where isnull(in_window)
| table _time, host, user, component
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained maintenance-window lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated Failed Firmware Update Attempts
description: Multiple firmware update attempts fail in succession — could indicate a corrupted/incompatible legitimate update, or repeated attempts to push an unsigned/tampered image past validation.
detection_logic: Counts firmware update failures per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="FirmwareUpdate" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count by host, _time
| where count>=3
tuning_guidance: Cross-reference with IDRAC-051 for validation-specific failures, which are higher priority than generic transfer/compatibility failures.
investigation_steps: Identify the failure reason for each attempt.
response_guidance: Investigate persistent failures, especially if any are validation-related.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Configuration Job Created
description: A Lifecycle Controller job is queued — covering firmware deployment, configuration application, OS deployment, or diagnostics. Jobs are the mechanism through which most Lifecycle-Controller-driven changes actually execute; this is the baseline detection for the higher-priority job-execution and import/export detections below.

data_sources.name: Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Job creation events with job type.

detection_logic: Filters the Lifecycle Log for job-creation events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="JobCreated"
| table _time, host, user, job_type
tuning_guidance: High-frequency, mostly-benign event — rely on the more specific detections below for alerting.
investigation_steps: Identify the job type and its intended scope.
response_guidance: No automatic action; feeds downstream detections.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Job Executed From Unusual Account
description: A Lifecycle Controller job executes under an account not on the small, expected list of deployment/automation identities that normally drive Lifecycle Controller activity (e.g. OpenManage Enterprise's service account).

data_sources.name: Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Job execution events cross-referenced against expected-operator baseline.

detection_logic: Joins job execution events against a lookup of expected Lifecycle Controller operator accounts.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="JobStarted"
| lookup idrac_lc_operators.csv user OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, host, user, job_type
tuning_guidance: Maintain the expected-operator lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification with the account owner.
response_guidance: Investigate and halt the job if unconfirmed and not yet complete.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Server Configuration Profile Imported
description: A Server Configuration Profile (a full XML/JSON export of iDRAC, BIOS, NIC, RAID, and boot configuration) is imported and applied. This can silently overwrite the device's entire configuration — accounts, boot settings, Secure Boot state, network configuration — in a single action, making it one of the highest-consequence single events this catalogue tracks, and one of the specification's explicitly named priority detections.

data_sources.name: Lifecycle Log
data_sources.description: Server Configuration Profile import events with source and target scope.

detection_logic: Filters the Lifecycle Log for Server Configuration Profile import events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="SCPImport"
| table _time, host, user, profile_source, target_scope
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for planned bulk configuration deployment/standardization via OpenManage Enterprise; require the profile_source to match an approved repository.
investigation_steps: Identify the profile source and diff it against the previous configuration to see exactly what changed.
Verify Secure Boot, TPM, boot order, and account roster after the import completes.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, restore from a known-good Server Configuration Profile backup and audit every configuration domain the import could have touched.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Server Configuration Profile Exported
description: A Server Configuration Profile is exported. Since the profile can contain configuration references to sensitive material (network settings, account structure, and in some export modes credential hashes), repeated or unusual-actor exports are a meaningful collection signal, the same reasoning applied to FortiManager configuration retrieval (FMG-021) in the Fortinet catalogue.
detection_logic: Filters the Lifecycle Log for Server Configuration Profile export events, counting distinct devices exported per user in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="SCPExport"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(host) as distinct_devices, values(host) as devices by user, _time
| where distinct_devices>=5
tuning_guidance: Expected for scheduled backup/configuration-management automation — allowlist the known automation account.
investigation_steps: Confirm the exporting account and business justification.
Check whether exported profiles were transferred off the management network.
response_guidance: Investigate as potential configuration/credential collection if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Hardware Inventory Modification
description: The Lifecycle Controller's recorded hardware inventory changes in a way inconsistent with a legitimate hardware add/replace event (e.g. component records disappearing without a corresponding maintenance ticket) — a soft signal that could indicate inventory data tampering intended to hide unauthorized hardware changes or removed components.
detection_logic: Filters the Lifecycle Log for inventory change events not correlated with a known maintenance ticket.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="InventoryChanged"
| lookup idrac_maintenance_windows.csv host _time OUTPUT in_window
| where isnull(in_window)
| table _time, host, component, change_type
tuning_guidance: High false-positive potential from routine hot-swap hardware events (disks, PSUs) — cross-reference with SEL hardware-removal events (IDRAC-072) for corroboration before treating as suspicious.
investigation_steps: Confirm against maintenance records.
Cross-reference with SEL for a corresponding physical event.
response_guidance: Investigate discrepancies between inventory records and physical reality.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1082: System Information Discovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lifecycle Controller Repeated Failed Jobs
description: Multiple Lifecycle Controller jobs fail in succession on the same device — could reflect a genuine automation/compatibility problem, or repeated attempts by an actor to push a configuration/firmware change that keeps failing validation.
detection_logic: Counts job failures per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_lc event="JobCompleted" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count, values(job_type) as job_types by host, _time
| where count>=3
tuning_guidance: Common during troubleshooting of a genuine automation issue — investigate the specific job_types before escalating.
investigation_steps: Review failure reasons for each job.
response_guidance: Investigate persistent failures for a security-relevant cause.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Redfish API Authentication Failures
description: Repeated Redfish API authentication failures. Redfish is the standards-based API increasingly used by automation/orchestration tooling to manage iDRAC — the same credential-guessing risk as the GUI/SSH interfaces applies, but attacks here are more likely to be scripted/automated given the API's design purpose.
detection_logic: Counts failed Redfish authentication attempts per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish event="SessionLogin" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count by host, src_ip, _time
| where count>=5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known automation source IPs whose retry logic may legitimately generate transient failures on token expiry.
investigation_steps: Validate the source against the automation-source allowlist.
response_guidance: Block the source; investigate the API client.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New Redfish API Client Source
description: A Redfish API session is authenticated from a source IP not on the known-automation allowlist. Since Redfish is designed for programmatic, unattended access, an unfamiliar client here is a stronger anomaly signal than an unfamiliar interactive GUI login would be.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Redfish session log
data_sources.description: API session events cross-referenced against an allowlist.

detection_logic: Joins Redfish session-start events against a known-client allowlist.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish event="SessionLogin" result="Success"
| lookup idrac_redfish_allowed_sources.csv src_ip OUTPUT is_allowed
| where isnull(is_allowed)
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Maintain the allowlist; this is one of the higher-precision anomaly signals in the catalogue given how static Redfish client populations typically are.
investigation_steps: Identify the client and confirm its purpose.
response_guidance: Revoke the session and rotate the credential if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Redfish API High-Volume Requests Against Sensitive Endpoints
description: A single API client generates an unusually high request volume against sensitive Redfish endpoints (`/redfish/v1/AccountService`, `/redfish/v1/Systems/{id}/Bios`, `/redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/VirtualMedia`) in a short window — consistent with automated enumeration/reconnaissance of the device's configuration surface ahead of a more targeted action.
detection_logic: Counts requests per (src_ip, api_uri-prefix) pair in a rolling window for sensitive endpoint categories.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish
| where match(api_uri, "(AccountService|Bios|VirtualMedia|SecureBoot)")
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count by src_ip, host, _time
| where count>=50
tuning_guidance: Exclude known monitoring/inventory tools that legitimately poll these endpoints on a schedule.
investigation_steps: Identify the client and its purpose.
response_guidance: Rate-limit or investigate the client if unexpected.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1082: System Information Discovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Redfish API Account Creation or Role Change
description: A new iDRAC account is created, or an existing account's role is changed, via a Redfish `POST`/`PATCH` to `/redfish/v1/AccountService/Accounts`. Functionally identical in impact to IDRAC-010/011, tracked separately here so API-driven account changes (which bypass the interactive GUI entirely and are easy to script at scale) are visible in their own right.
detection_logic: Filters Redfish API log for POST/PATCH methods against the AccountService/Accounts endpoint.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish api_uri="*AccountService/Accounts*" api_method IN ("POST","PATCH")
| table _time, host, src_ip, api_uri, api_method
tuning_guidance: Correlate with change management for legitimate API-driven provisioning.
investigation_steps: Identify exactly which account was created/changed and to what role.
response_guidance: Disable/downgrade immediately if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Redfish API Virtual Media Mount or Boot Override
description: A virtual media mount or boot-override action is issued via the Redfish API — the API-driven equivalent of the IDRAC-030/037 GUI-console attack chain. API-driven media/boot manipulation is easier to script and repeat across a fleet than console interaction, making it the preferred path for an automated attack tool.

data_sources.name: iDRAC Redfish API log
data_sources.description: Virtual media and boot-configuration API calls.

detection_logic: Filters Redfish API log for POST/PATCH methods against VirtualMedia and Boot-related endpoints.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish (api_uri="*VirtualMedia*" OR api_uri="*/Boot*") api_method IN ("POST","PATCH")
| table _time, host, src_ip, api_uri, api_method
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for automated OS deployment tooling using the Redfish API — allowlist known deployment automation clients.
investigation_steps: Treat with the same urgency as IDRAC-030/032 — trace the full API session for a subsequent reboot.
response_guidance: Same response posture as IDRAC-032: power off and investigate if the sequence is unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1200 (Hardware Additions) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-030.

title: Redfish API Log Service Cleared
description: The Redfish `LogServices` endpoint is used to clear the Lifecycle Log or System Event Log via API. Since this catalogue's own visibility depends on this log surviving, an API-driven log-clear is treated with the same urgency as the syslog-redirection and log-purge detections in the Fortinet and Red Hat catalogues.
detection_logic: Filters Redfish API log for POST calls against the LogServices Actions/ClearLog endpoint. Because the very log being queried may be the one cleared, this detection depends on external syslog forwarding surviving the clear action (see IDRAC-060).
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_redfish api_uri="*LogServices*ClearLog*" api_method="POST"
| table _time, host, src_ip, api_uri
tuning_guidance: No routine legitimate case outside a documented log-rotation procedure — require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Identify what preceded the clear action using any externally-forwarded syslog copy.
Treat the clearing session as highly suspect.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed anti-forensics incident pending explicit authorization evidence.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RACADM Remote Connection Established
description: A remote RACADM session connects to the device. RACADM exposes nearly the full breadth of iDRAC configuration as scriptable CLI commands, making it functionally equivalent in power to the GUI/Redfish API but with less structured per-command logging in some firmware versions.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for remote RACADM session events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="RACADMSession"
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected automation source IPs.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference src_ip against the automation/jump-host allowlist.
response_guidance: No automatic action for expected sources; investigate per IDRAC-006 if outside the OOB network.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RACADM User or Password Modification Command
description: A RACADM command modifying a user account or password (`racadm set iDRAC.Users`) is executed. Tracked distinctly from the GUI-driven IDRAC-010/011 detections because RACADM's scriptable nature makes it the preferred mechanism for an attacker automating account changes across many devices at once.
detection_logic: Filters the RACADM command log for commands targeting the iDRAC.Users configuration group.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_racadm command="*set iDRAC.Users*"
| table _time, host, user, command
tuning_guidance: Correlate with change management for legitimate scripted provisioning.
investigation_steps: Parse the command for exactly which attribute was changed (UserName, Password, Enable, Privilege).
response_guidance: Reverse unauthorized changes and rotate affected credentials immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RACADM BIOS or Boot Configuration Command
description: A RACADM command modifying BIOS settings or boot configuration (`racadm set BIOS.*`, `racadm jobqueue create` targeting a BIOS config job) is executed — scriptable, fleet-scale equivalent of IDRAC-037 through IDRAC-042.
detection_logic: Filters the RACADM command log for commands targeting the BIOS configuration group.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_racadm command="*set BIOS.*"
| table _time, host, user, command
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for scripted fleet BIOS-standardization deployments — require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Parse the command for the specific setting changed (SecureBoot, TpmSecurity, BootMode all warrant immediate escalation).
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized changes; escalate immediately if the setting is Secure Boot or TPM.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Same T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) closest-fit rationale as IDRAC-037.

title: RACADM Configuration Export or Import Command
description: A RACADM `get -f` (export) or `set -f` (import) full-configuration command is executed — the CLI equivalent of LC-003/LC-004's Server Configuration Profile import/export.
detection_logic: Filters the RACADM command log for `get -f` and `set -f` configuration file operations.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_racadm (command="get -f *" OR command="set -f *")
| table _time, host, user, command
tuning_guidance: Same reasoning as LC-003/LC-004 — legitimate for automation, but every import deserves diffing against the prior configuration.
investigation_steps: For an import, diff against the prior configuration.
For an export, confirm business justification and destination.
response_guidance: Same as LC-003/LC-004.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System

author: Threat Detection Library

title: RACADM Reset or Factory Default Command
description: A RACADM `racreset` or `racadm racresetcfg` command is executed, resetting iDRAC to factory defaults. The CLI equivalent of IDRAC-090's factory-reset detection.
detection_logic: Filters the RACADM command log for reset/factory-default commands.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_racadm (command="racreset*" OR command="racresetcfg")
| table _time, host, user, command
tuning_guidance: No tuning — this should never occur on a production device outside a fully-documented decommissioning process.
investigation_steps: Confirm against decommissioning records immediately.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed incident if unaccounted for; preserve any externally-forwarded logs before they age out.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI Authentication Failure / Brute Force
description: Repeated IPMI authentication failures. IPMI is an older, less-hardened out-of-band management protocol than Redfish, with known cipher-suite weaknesses (see IPMI-005) — where still enabled, it deserves the same brute-force detection coverage as every other iDRAC access path.
detection_logic: Counts failed IPMI authentication attempts per device in a rolling window.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_ipmi event="Login" result="Failed"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count by host, src_ip, _time
| where count>=5
tuning_guidance: Minimal legitimate tuning expected.
investigation_steps: Validate the source against the automation-source allowlist.
response_guidance: Block the source; consider whether IPMI needs to remain enabled at all given its weaker security model relative to Redfish.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI Chassis Power Action
description: A chassis power action (on/off/cycle/reset) is issued via IPMI. The IPMI-specific equivalent of IDRAC-034 — tracked separately since IPMI power control may bypass some of the auditing/authorization refinements available through the newer Redfish/GUI paths.
detection_logic: Filters the IPMI log for chassis power control commands.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_ipmi event="ChassisControl"
| table _time, host, src_ip, action
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected automation source IPs.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexpected; same posture as IDRAC-034.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI User Account Changes
description: An IPMI user account is created or modified. IPMI maintains its own user table, which can be a separate persistence surface from iDRAC's own account list depending on firmware version and configuration — an attacker could create an IPMI-only account that doesn't show up in a GUI-focused account audit.
detection_logic: Filters the IPMI log for user account creation/modification events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_ipmi event="UserSet"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: No routine legitimate ongoing pattern outside initial provisioning.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference the IPMI user table against the main iDRAC account roster — any IPMI-only account is inherently suspicious.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized IPMI accounts immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI Over LAN Enabled
description: IPMI-over-LAN access is enabled where it was previously disabled. Given IPMI's known protocol-level weaknesses (RAKP hash disclosure, weak cipher suites), many hardening guides recommend disabling it entirely in favor of Redfish/HTTPS — re-enabling it reopens an attack surface deliberately closed.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for IPMI-over-LAN enablement events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="IPMILan" cfgattr_value="Enabled"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Legitimate only where a specific, documented tool requires IPMI specifically over Redfish — require a change ticket and a compensating cipher-suite hardening review (IPMI-005).
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification; verify strong cipher suites are enforced if IPMI must remain enabled.
response_guidance: Disable IPMI-over-LAN again unless explicitly justified.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1599: Network Boundary Bridging

author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI Weak Cipher Suite in Use
description: An IPMI session negotiates or is configured to allow a weak/null cipher suite (notably Cipher Suite 0, which requires no authentication at all). Cipher Suite 0 in particular is a well-documented, historically-exploited IPMI weakness that effectively provides unauthenticated access.

data_sources.name: iDRAC IPMI log
data_sources.description: Cipher suite configuration and session negotiation records.

detection_logic: Filters IPMI configuration/session events for weak or null cipher suite usage.
spl:
index=idrac (sourcetype=idrac_ipmi event="SessionNegotiate") OR (sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="IPMICipherSuite")
| where cipher_suite="0" OR match(cipher_suite,"(?i)(none|null)")
| table _time, host, cipher_suite
tuning_guidance: No legitimate case for Cipher Suite 0 remaining enabled — this should fail a security baseline check outright.
investigation_steps: Disable Cipher Suite 0 and any other weak ciphers immediately upon discovery.
response_guidance: Harden cipher suite configuration fleet-wide; treat any observed use of Cipher Suite 0 as a potential unauthenticated-access incident.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPMI Serial-Over-LAN (SOL) Session
description: A Serial-Over-LAN session is started via IPMI, providing text-console access to the host's serial console — the IPMI equivalent of the iDRAC Virtual Console (IDRAC-020), with the same fundamental ability to interact with the host outside normal network access controls.
detection_logic: Filters the IPMI log for SOL session-start events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_ipmi event="SOLSessionStart"
| table _time, host, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Same baselining approach as IDRAC-020/021.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a change ticket or known maintenance activity.
response_guidance: Same posture as unexpected Virtual Console access (IDRAC-021).
author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Network Interface Moved to Unexpected VLAN or Address Range
description: The iDRAC's own IP address, subnet, gateway, or VLAN assignment changes to a value outside the expected out-of-band management range. Since this is the address administrators (and this catalogue's own detections) use to reach the device, an unexpected change can both expose it to a broader network and disrupt legitimate monitoring.
detection_logic: Filters network configuration changes and validates the new address/VLAN against the expected OOB range.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("IPv4Address","VLANID","Gateway")
| lookup idrac_oob_cidrs.csv new_value AS ip_check OUTPUT is_oob_range
| where isnull(is_oob_range)
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr, new_value
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during planned network re-addressing; require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Verify the new network placement against the intended OOB architecture.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized changes immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1599: Network Boundary Bridging

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Shared LOM Mode Enabled
description: The iDRAC NIC selection is changed from a dedicated out-of-band management port to shared LOM mode, where management traffic rides the same physical NIC as production/host traffic. This is the single configuration change most likely to expose iDRAC to a network segment it was never intended to be reachable from.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for NIC selection changes to a shared/LOM mode.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="NicSelection" cfgattr_value IN ("Shared","SharedWithFailover")
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Some environments deliberately run shared LOM to reduce cabling — if so, treat as a documented exception, not a finding, but still confirm segmentation (VLAN tagging) compensates.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Verify VLAN segmentation compensates if shared mode is intentional.
response_guidance: Revert to dedicated NIC mode unless explicitly justified and compensated.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1599: Network Boundary Bridging

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC SSH or HTTPS Service Newly Enabled
description: A management service (SSH, HTTPS on a non-default port) is enabled where it was previously disabled, or its listening port is changed.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for service enable/port configuration changes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("SSHEnable","HTTPSPort","SSHPort")
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during initial provisioning; require a change ticket post-deployment.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1599: Network Boundary Bridging

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Session Timeout Weakened
description: The GUI/SSH/RACADM session idle-timeout setting is increased or disabled, extending how long an authenticated session remains active without interaction — the iDRAC equivalent of FGT-017.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for session-timeout configuration changes.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr="Timeout"
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: Legitimate for troubleshooting long-running console operations; require a change ticket for a permanent increase.
investigation_steps: Determine whether the change was reverted after a maintenance window.
response_guidance: Revert to the organizational standard timeout if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556.004: Network Device Authentication

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Certificate Replaced or CA Trust Added
description: The iDRAC's HTTPS server certificate is replaced, or a new trusted CA is imported. A rogue trusted CA addition can let an attacker mint certificates iDRAC will present as valid, undermining an administrator's ability to verify they're actually connecting to the genuine device.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for certificate import/replacement events.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="CertificateImport"
| table _time, host, user, cert_type
tuning_guidance: Legitimate during certificate renewal cycles; require a change ticket and verify the fingerprint against the expected issuer.
investigation_steps: Verify the certificate's issuing CA and fingerprint.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized trusted CAs immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1553.004: Install Root Certificate

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Self-Signed Certificate Generated Unexpectedly
description: A new self-signed certificate is generated on a device where a CA-issued certificate is the organizational standard — could indicate a rollback to weaker trust posture, whether accidental or deliberate.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for self-signed certificate generation on devices flagged as requiring CA-issued certificates.
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="CertificateGenerated" cert_type="SelfSigned"
| lookup idrac_ca_required.csv host OUTPUT requires_ca
| where requires_ca="true"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Legitimate as a temporary fallback during a CA outage — confirm this isn't the case before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether this was an intentional fallback or an unauthorized downgrade.
response_guidance: Reissue a CA-signed certificate promptly.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1553.004: Install Root Certificate

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Remote Syslog Forwarding Disabled or Destination Changed
description: Remote syslog forwarding is disabled, or its destination is changed. Because this catalogue's own visibility into iDRAC depends on this forwarding path reaching Splunk, disabling or redirecting it is one of the highest-priority anti-forensics actions available to an attacker — named explicitly by the specification alongside SEL clearing and log-service clearing.
detection_logic: Filters the iDRAC audit log for syslog forwarding configuration changes. Because this event may itself be the last one forwarded before redirection takes effect, treat any gap in expected heartbeat/audit traffic from a device as a secondary signal (see IDRAC-067).
spl:
index=idrac sourcetype=idrac_audit event="ConfigChange" cfgattr IN ("SyslogEnable","SyslogServer")
| table _time, host, user, cfgattr
tuning_guidance: No routine legitimate case for disabling syslog forwarding outright; server-address changes should map to a documented SIEM migration.
investigation_steps: Verify the new destination (if changed, not disabled) is known, owned infrastructure.
Check for any other suspicious activity immediately before this change — it is frequently the first step in a broader compromise.
response_guidance: Restore forwarding immediately; treat the acting session as compromised until proven otherwise.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1601: Modify System Image

author: Threat Detection Library

title: iDRAC Device Silent — No Audit Log Received in Expected Interval
description: A device that normally sends periodic heartbeat/audit events stops appearing in the log stream entirely. This is a compensating detection for the case where syslog forwarding was disabled (IDRAC-066) so cleanly that the disabling event itself never arrived, or where the network path was cut rather than the configuration changed.

data_sources.name: iDRAC audit log (absence)
data_sources.path: n/a — computed from expected vs. observed device presence
